clue.text: It's another place to peer, for example

definitions.text: It's another place to peer, for example

parts.words: It's another place to peer, for example
parts.note: members of the House of Lords traditionally refer to the lower chamber as 'another place' rather than by name, so to a peer this chamber is that other place

explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a verb about looking; it is a member of the House of Lords, for whom 'another place' is the parliamentary euphemism for the elected chamber.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliamentary etiquette has peers call the elected lower chamber 'another place', so the clue's phrase is that chamber's nickname in the Lords.

clue.text: Smug head office tour in health resort

indicators.note: to re-sort is to sort again, so the letters of these words are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A smug executive from head office makes an inspection tour of a spa town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Health resort' reads as a spa; 'resort' is really the instruction to sort the letters of TOUR IN HEALTH again, giving LIERTHANTHOU.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone holier-than-thou acts morally superior, a self-satisfied, sanctimonious smugness.

clue.text: Release Blue Berets with roles on way north

parts.note: United Nations peacekeepers wear blue berets, so they stand for UN

indicators.note: in a down clue, travelling north means reading upwards, so the word is written backwards

parts.note: an actor's roles are parts

explanation.surface: UN peacekeepers are released from their duties and sent off northwards in new roles.
explanation.definitionFit: To unstrap something is to undo its straps and so free or release it.

clue.text: It grows down river in Germany

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the ... duck, whose soft down feathers fill eiderdowns
second meaning: the ..., a river in Schleswig-Holstein, northern Germany

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grows down' tempts you to think of a plant growing downwards or a river flowing down; it is a bird growing soft feathers.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a sea duck prized for its fine down, and the Eider is also a northern German river flowing into the North Sea.

clue.text: Big boxer stumped believer in Murphy's Law?

parts.note: big means fat
Muhammad Ali, the famous heavyweight boxer
ST is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for stumped

explanation.surface: A heavyweight fighter, beaten by a question, concludes that whatever can go wrong will.
explanation.walkthrough: Murphy's Law says anything that can go wrong will; the question mark admits that a fatalist believes outcomes are fixed rather than specifically bad.
explanation.definitionFit: A fatalist accepts that events are predetermined and inevitable, close in spirit to expecting the worst to happen.

clue.text: Delayed using horse past its best?

parts.note: a drug user is said to be 'on' something
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H
something past its best is old

explanation.surface: A race is postponed because the horse entered is too old to run.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures an aged racehorse; 'using horse' is drug slang, ON heroin.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan put on hold is postponed or suspended, that is, delayed until later.

clue.text: Base trickery takes in husband for now

parts.note: base means mean or low

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so the husband's letter goes within

parts.note: wiles are tricks, so wile is trickery

explanation.surface: A low trick fools a husband for the time being.
explanation.definitionFit: Meanwhile means in the intervening time, for the present moment, the same as for now.

clue.text: Annoying hack working, missing nothing

parts.note: a hack is a worn-out horse, a nag

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so the letter for nothing is dropped

parts.note: a machine that is working is going
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A tiresome journalist goes on working but produces nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' suggests a hack writer; here it is an old horse, a NAG. 'Missing' drops the O (nothing) from GOING, leaving GING.
explanation.definitionFit: Nagging means persistently irritating, as a nagging pain or complaint is annoying.

clue.text: Attlee's and Mr Eden's revised appropriate appellation?

definitions.text: Attlee's and Mr Eden's revised appropriate appellation?

indicators.note: something revised has been reworked, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters ATTLEES
taken as written, the letters MREDENS

explanation.surface: Former prime ministers Clement Attlee and Anthony Eden have their names revised into a fitting title.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram uses only the letters of the two names; 'and' simply joins them. Attlee and Eden were both senior post-war British prime ministers, so the phrase their names make suits them.
explanation.definitionFit: Elder statesmen are respected retired politicians, a fitting description of two former prime ministers.

clue.text: Desperate stand by dump

parts.note: to stand something is to last or endure it
to dump something is to ditch it

explanation.surface: A desperate stand is made beside a rubbish tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' looks like part of the phrase 'last stand'; it is LAST alone, with 'by' joining it to DITCH.
explanation.definitionFit: A last-ditch effort is a final desperate attempt made when all else has failed.

clue.text: Sponsor a northern set

parts.note: jelly that has set has gelled, so set means gel

explanation.surface: A sponsor backs a northern television set or team.
explanation.definitionFit: An angel is a financial backer, especially one who funds a theatrical production.

clue.text: X marks this first in English, zero in the three Rs

indicators.note: the first letter of the word that follows
zero goes inside the three Rs

parts.note: the three Rs are reading, writing and arithmetic, here simply three letter Rs
zero is the letter O

explanation.surface: A teacher's cross marks the first mistake in English or a zero among the basics.
explanation.walkthrough: The three Rs (reading, writing and arithmetic) are the basics of schooling; here they are literally RRR, with O put among them.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacher marks a mistake with a cross, so X marks a wrong answer.

clue.text: Immaculate story about extremely lousy trifle

indicators.note: the lie goes around the other letters

parts.note: a story can be a lie

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: a whit is a tiny amount, a trifle

explanation.surface: A spotless tale is told about a rather lousy pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trifle' suggests the British layered pudding of sponge, custard and cream; here it means a tiny amount.
explanation.definitionFit: Lily-white means pure white, and by extension morally spotless or blameless.

clue.text: Kind acts somehow filling familiar role

parts.note: a kind is a type

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A kind actor somehow ends up in the same old part again.
explanation.definitionFit: A typecast actor is repeatedly given the same kind of part, always playing a character type audiences already know.

clue.text: Temperature aside, glass is protecting hot young flyer

indicators.note: the remaining letters wrap around the letter for hot
set aside means removed, so the T comes out

parts.note: crystal is fine glass
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Whatever the temperature, a glass case protects a delicate young insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Young flyer' is not a child pilot but an insect not yet able to fly; 'aside' tells you to set the temperature letter apart from the glass.
explanation.definitionFit: A chrysalis is the pupa of a butterfly or moth, the stage before it emerges as a winged insect.

clue.text: Graduates collect ten grand for green fuel

indicators.note: to collect is to gather in, so the graduates hold the other letters

parts.note: BAs are Bachelors of Arts, graduates
10 written as the letters IO
G is slang shorthand for a grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: Graduates raise ten thousand pounds for an eco-friendly fuel project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ten grand' reads as ten thousand pounds; it splits into 10 (IO) and G for grand.
explanation.definitionFit: Biogas is methane-rich gas made from rotting organic matter, a renewable and environmentally friendly fuel.

clue.text: What occupant of 25 does, with mixture in vessel

indicators.note: the mixture is placed in the vessel, so its letters go inside

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, a vessel
a welter is a confused mass or jumble, a mixture

explanation.surface: A recipe step: someone in the steam room mixes something in a bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 25 is STEAM ROOM. 'Vessel' suggests a bowl; it is SS, a steamship, with WELTER placed in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sitting in a steam room is uncomfortably hot and sweats heavily, which is sweltering.

clue.text: Sign a posh wig should be returned by end of day

parts.note: U means upper-class, the posh sense in 'U and non-U'

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: rug is slang for a wig or toupee

indicators.note: the last letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A notice says a smart wig must be brought back by close of business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rug' is slang for a toupee. 'Posh' is U, from the old division of speech into upper-class U and non-U.
explanation.definitionFit: An augury is an omen, a sign of what is to come.

clue.text: Baltic golf learners welcoming a bunch of spies

parts.note: G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: to welcome is to take in, so the learners hold the next letters

parts.note: L is the learner plate on a British car, so two learners are LL
the CIA is the American intelligence agency, a group of spies

explanation.surface: Novice golfers on a freezing northern course are joined by a group of spies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baltic' is British slang for freezing cold, not the sea; 'learners' come from the L-plates British learner drivers display.
explanation.definitionFit: Baltic is informal British slang for bitterly cold, and glacial means icy, extremely cold.

clue.text: Time fitted in to brush each scented plant

indicators.note: the letter for time is put inside the word for brush

parts.note: to brush a floor is to sweep it

explanation.surface: Someone finds time to brush every fragrant plant in the garden.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet pea is a climbing garden flower grown for its strongly fragrant blooms.

clue.text: Two features in green type of camera

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a golf green has a pin (the flagstick) and a hole, two features that together name the word
second meaning: a lensless camera admitting light through a tiny hole

explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' suggests colour or environmentalism; it is a putting green on a golf course, whose two features run together into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinhole camera has no lens, letting light in through a tiny aperture to form an image.

clue.text: A snooty sort erected current plant

indicators.note: erected means built upright, so in a down clue the words read upwards, backwards

parts.note: a snob is a snooty person
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A snooty person has built an electrical power plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current plant' suggests a power station; 'plant' alone is the definition, a growing one.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonsai is a tree or shrub kept miniature by careful pruning, grown as a potted plant.

clue.text: Despicable type's excessively large growth capped

parts.note: a toad is a contemptible person, and the 's adds S
excessively means too
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A despicable person's oversized growth has been capped.
explanation.definitionFit: A toadstool is a fungus with a cap on a stalk, a growth with a cap on top.

clue.text: One's present part of course entertains Poles

indicators.note: to entertain is to host, so the tee holds the poles inside

parts.note: a tee is part of a golf course, where each hole starts
N and S are the north and south poles, the two poles together

explanation.surface: Someone's gift, part of a course, plays host to Polish visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' suggests Polish people; they are the two magnetic poles, N and S. 'One's present' means present is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The present is a grammatical tense, the verb form describing what is happening now.

clue.text: Perhaps watch sphere from the south

indicators.note: in a down clue, reading from the bottom means reading upwards, backwards

parts.note: a remit is an area of responsibility, a sphere

explanation.surface: Someone watches a globe from the southern hemisphere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sphere' suggests a ball; it means a sphere of authority, a REMIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A watch is one example of a timer, a device measuring elapsed time; 'perhaps' signals the example.

clue.text: Oxford college or one the Spanish added

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Choosing between an Oxford college and one the Spaniards added to the university.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriel College is one of the constituent colleges of the University of Oxford.

clue.text: Staunch Arab, back installing a place for sweaters

indicators.note: to install is to put in, so the stem holds the letter

parts.note: to staunch a flow of blood is to stem it

indicators.note: back means reversed, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: a Moor is a North African Arab

explanation.surface: A loyal Arab returns and fits out a place to keep jumpers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweaters' suggests jumpers, the British word for knitted sweaters; here they are people who sweat. 'Staunch' is the verb, to STEM.
explanation.definitionFit: A steam room is a heated room filled with steam where people go to sweat.

clue.text: Corpulent sags I reconstructed?

indicators.note: something reconstructed is rebuilt in a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cosmetic surgeon remarks on rebuilding an overweight patient's sagging body.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the anagram and the description: the person who reconstructs sagging flesh.
explanation.definitionFit: A plastic surgeon reshapes and repairs the body, including tightening sagging skin on an overweight patient.
